utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: First it was the SDS, headed by Miroslav Deronjic, that requested this. There were a few activists there, headed by Miroslav Deronjic. They came to the office of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence. They asked for these lists. However, since he did not have the power of his command in charge to hand over these lists, he did not give them to them. They threatened him and then he was compelled to call the police to help him, and of course the police had to intervene, to come there and to provide security for his office at the municipality, things like that. The activists of the Serb Democratic Party thus failed but then a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army came from Ljubovija, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Gusic. Now, was it from Serbia or from somewhere else, but at that rate wasn't the Yugoslav People's Army the Yugoslav People's Army throughout the territory of Yugoslavia? So there was not a JNA of Serbia or a JNA of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I'm just telling you they came from Serbia. That unit came from Serbia. We know that. We know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that things were somewhat different, that actually the army was supposed to take over this entire documentation according to a decision reached by the federal government, not according to the decision of any kind of SDS activists from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, then the activists of the SDS should be asked why they wanted to take this file away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were just supporting the decisions reached by the federal government and they were trying to make sure that this be handed over to the army, not to them. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: That was not my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Even if this were not your understanding, you nevertheless remember what happened, that is, that the SDA collected a considerable number of people and then you set up a roadblock around the municipality building and then there was the JNA on the other side and they wanted to take over these documents on the basis of the decision of the federal government. What about this roadblock? Was it actually facing the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: First of all, the SDS rallied the Serb people together, because the activists of the SDS headed by Miroslav Deronjic, they did not manage to take these files away. Then the activists of the SDA called upon the people to gather at a rally in front of the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac with a view to supporting the activists of the Serb Democratic Party, that pressure be brought to bear against Dzemail Becirevic, secretary of the Secretariat of the National Defence, to hand over these card files. However, at that time the police was protecting the municipality. We from the SDA, in view of the fact that it was a market day, Friday, in Bratunac, there were quite a few people who had come from the rural areas to do their buying and selling on that day. The news spread round among the people, this that had to do with the files, and then the Muslim people rallied together and they gave support to the legal government, the legally elected government of the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac. And when the army came, on the one side were Muslims and in front of these Muslims there was the legal police protecting the legal authorities of the Municipality of Bratunac, and on the other side was the army. That unit of the Yugoslav People's Army, with all its weapons, and behind the army was a rather large mass of Serb civilians that were extending their support to the unit of the Yugoslav People's Army. So this was a very unpleasant atmosphere with high tensions, and it culminated when the major, who led this unit, issued an order to fire, and this was done. There were a few bursts of gunfire that were shot above the heads of the people who had gathered there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us see what you wrote here in your statement. At the end of paragraph -- of page 3. "This JNA unit was commanded by a major whose name I do not know. He made threats and began shouting and arguing, again demanding that the files be handed over." So the JNA asked for the list to be handed over, not the Serb Democratic Party. And then you say, "He was joined by SDS officials and Serb police officers and some Serb civilians who happened to be in the street." And then we move on to the next page: "And the whole situation escalated and I had a great sense of foreboding of what might happen." And then you say: "We had a crowd of approximately two to four thousand who remained adamant that they would not allow the JNA access to the municipality building. Soon after that the order -- the soldiers were ordered to fire into the air but we remained resolute and eventually the officer withdrew his soldiers and left, having failed to appropriate the files that he wanted." Is that what happened? The JNA, according to the decision reached by the federal government, asked for documentation that had to do with the military obligation. You surrounded the municipality building by citizens, and they fired into the air in order to make it possible for them to carry out their assignment. However, they did not want to clash with the citizens and then they withdrew without having completed their assignment. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: There is something that was added to this other page in the statement, and I spelled it out in more specific terms, and it's the way I've been saying here into this microphone. Of course, that's not to say, on the other hand, that what is written in this statement does not portray a picture of what I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I just quoted your very own statement to you.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: But there is an addendum. I talked to investigators here and I added something to this statement and I think you should have this addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not waste time over these details now. Is it correct that the first misunderstandings and conflicts in the Municipal Assembly actually came about because of the recognition or non-recognition of the SFRY authorities and their decisions? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what you've been saying here about the conflict that had to do with the handover of military documents, is that the reason why this happened? It had to do with the recognition of the state authorities and organs of the SFRY and its decisions?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: At that time this was high politics for me. I know that the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence did not have the authority from the command in charge to hand over these files, so these were the legal authorities at the time, and he respected the orders of his superiors and he acted according to these orders. As for the decision of the federal government, believe me, I don't know of its existence and I don't even know whether it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see here, the army asked for these documents and you prevented them from taking these documents and the Serbs supported the decision of the federal authorities, that these documents should be taken, that is. Is that what it boils down to, or are you trying to say something else?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that the Serbs were supporting the federal government authorities. Quite simply, the Muslims were afraid that these files would be taken away, and this was supposed to be used for forced mobilisation and to send these people to the frontline in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it was to be used for sending reservists to Croatia if this was a federal government decision that the army should take over files concerning military conscripts? How would you know that this was done in order to send military reservists to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I know that at that time there was some fighting at the frontlines in Croatia. Military conscripts were sent to the frontlines in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you linked that up to the decision of the federal government to have the documentation taken over.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about this federal government decision. Please don't ask me about it all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you say that the JNA had placed heavy artillery and mortars above the hills -- on the hills above Bratunac with the barrels facing town and that in the village of Vranesevici the JNA regular units were training local Serb civilians and that SDA activists went there to see with their own eyes these particular activities and then they duly reported that back to you. First of all, tell me, do you know for sure where the JNA units were and why this was so?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I know for sure that they were positioned in Vranesevici and that they were carrying out the training of Serb civilians to use weapons. We had information from several sources. I already said that one of the sources were the activists of the SDA who went there to see it with their own eyes. Another source were local people from the area around these villages, that is to say, the Muslim inhabitants of these villages that were near Vranesevici. And the third report came officially from the chief of police. He sent the police to the actual site. At first we did not know which JNA unit this was, and it is for that reason that the executive board of the SDA of Bratunac officially requested from the president of the Municipal Assembly, Nijaz Ljubicic, and the secretary, the municipal secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence, Dzemail Becirevic, to go to the military command in charge in Tuzla and to ask how come there was a JNA unit training Serb civilians in the village of Vranesevici in the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the answer you got was that they did not know about this, that any such training was being carried out or that there is any such JNA unit that was within the Tuzla Corps. How come the unit was there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: The answer we got was that they did not know about this, that they would check it out within three days, and that within three days they would come to the municipality of Bratunac and that they would do their best to have these problems overcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, were these problems overcome?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: After three days, they did not come to Bratunac but they telephoned, saying that this was not a unit from Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather, that this was a unit from Serbia, a unit of the JNA from Serbia and that they were not in charge in any way and they could not influence this in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these people who said that they were not in charge were also in the command of the corps in Tuzla, the JNA corps; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the JNA said to you that they were not in charge of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this connection, did a meeting take place afterwards between your representatives and the SDS, and is it correct that in connection with the entire situation in Bratunac it was precisely you and the president of the SDS of Bratunac that issued a joint statement in order to reassure the population that everything would be just fine?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: You see, this statement was made on behalf of all the citizens present at that rally that was held in view of the complex political and security situation in the municipality of Bratunac. On behalf of the SDA and on behalf of the SDS, there were the five top people present respectively, and all the other citizens were represented too, so this was a statement made on behalf of all the citizens. Our aim was to reassure the citizens, stating that solutions would be found in terms of future peaceful co-existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was your joint statement and your joint position at the time.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Of all the citizens who attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Serbs, the Muslims, the representatives of the SDS, and the representatives of the SDA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No exceptions?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: No exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what you say on page 4 in paragraph 9, is that correct that the president of the SDS of Bratunac said to you then that the Serbs felt that they were a minority and they felt jeopardised because of the pressure that is exerted upon them by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: He said that the Serbs in Bratunac were a minority and they could only trust the Serb police, that they could not trust anyone else, that there were some stories going round that Serbs could be jeopardised and that he wants to provide adequate security to the Serb people in terms of any possible jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he express concern then over developments in other parts of Bosnia due to the information that was coming in that Muslim units called the Green Berets were coming to Bratunac? You talk about that too in your statement.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: He referred to the Green Berets, but he was aware himself that in Bratunac there were never any Green Berets or any kind of organisation that could upset these inter-ethnic relations, as regards the Muslim side, that is. He said this in order to achieve his objective; namely, to divide the police. That was the task he had, and he admitted it later, that Radovan Karadzic strongly pressured him to have the police in Bratunac divided into the Serb police and the Muslim police. Later on we found out why this was done, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, during the abbreviated examination-in-chief, you said that a friend of yours said that a friend of his had spoke to Radovan Karadzic and said that Bosnia should be divided and -- who is this friend of yours who talked to Karadzic, and who is it that he told that Bosnia should be divided?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Osman Brka. You probably know him. At that time he was one of the top men in the SDA and he was there in headquarters and I think that he was an MP as well, and he told me that in the building where the SDA and the SDS were he happened to meet Karadzic in the hall and that Karadzic said that to him, that the Serb people should be separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he told you about his alleged conversation with Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that Karadzic had said to him that this should be done, that this had to be done. And then he asked, "How could that be done? Do you see these big buildings here? Serbs live there. Bosniaks, Muslims, many others, and it's impossible to do that." And he said, "It has to be done. It has to be done."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, this was before the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when was that, roughly? Will you try and recollect.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it during the time when there were negotiations on the plan that was known as the Cutilheiro Plan? Was that in those days?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: It was much earlier. I don't know exactly, but it was much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you're unable to locate the event in time, tell me, since you mentioned the incident in which two Muslims were killed and two were wounded, was this the reason that resulted in the arrival of members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina coming, one Serb, one Muslim, that is, Nikola Koljevic and Ejub Ganic? Was that the motive for their arrival?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the 4th of April, did Vitomir Zepinic, Deputy Minister of the Interior, and Avdo Hebib, advisor, and Enver Saric, chief of the Department of the Security Service in Tuzla, arrive as well, that is, a day prior to the arrival of Koljevic and Ganic? As I see Zepinic, Avdo Hebib, and Enver Saric, did they come also clearly to try and appeal the situation, to calm things down?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: You see, this was not on the 4th of April. You said it was the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: The 4th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 4th of September. Yes, I'm sorry. I made a mistake in the month.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: It is true that they came in order to calm the situation down in Bratunac municipality and that their arrival was a function of that -- those efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, and just then, in connection with the barricade that you mentioned, there were constant Muslim roadblocks in the villages of Glogova, Branca, and Pervani. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac, up to the 17th of April, while I was there, there were no Muslim barricades in any part of Bratunac or in any part of the municipality of Bratunac. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not in Glogova, Branca, or Pervani, there were no Muslim roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: No, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is not true that vehicles of public transport were intercepted, citizens asked to show their IDs and so on? You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I do know that it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that on one occasion in Pervani, the Serbs were forced out of a bus and the leader of the roadblock was Mehmed Alija Selimovic who boasted that he had attended wartime training in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: This was in the autumn of 1991. I don't remember that, and I don't believe that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And at the beginning of February 1992, was a meeting held of representatives of the SDA of Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, and Vlasenica? Those from Gorazde couldn't come and the meeting was held at the hunting lodge near Srebrenica and the subject was preparations for war. This is also in Besim Ibisevic's book, and at the time you were president of the municipal board in Bratunac or was it your predecessor? This was February 1992.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: If this was in February 1992, I was not president of the municipal board of the SDA in Bratunac at that time, so I really don't know that this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what were you then when Kavazbasic was president?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the executive board of the SDA and one of the three vice-presidents of the executive board of the SDA of Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you as the vice-president were not aware of a meeting held in February 1992 of presidents and representatives of SDA of Srebrenica, Zvornik, and Vlasenica. You know nothing about --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I certainly didn't know about it nor did I know that it was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever read this book by Besim Ibisevic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I heard that he had written a book, but I don't know what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that it was precisely in those days, that is, beginning of 1992, that weapons were stolen from JNA depots? Do you remember that even a gun was stolen, a cannon, in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: And where? Where? You mean in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that area.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is also mentioned in that same book by Besim Ibisevic, this event. As you say that you hadn't read the book, I'm not asking you whether you saw it in the book, I'm asking you whether you remember the event he describes.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac there were no cannon. I don't remember that anyone had taken a cannon from anyone, that is, that any Muslim had done that. I hear that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally armed, Mr. Gusic, tell me, in 1991/1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Apart from the pistol I had, I was not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had a legal pistol with a licence and you opened fire with it, again legally?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I opened fire with my pistol when I had to, when my life was in danger, as is explained in that statement of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And with that shooting, was that intimidation and did people start to move out? You speak about that in paragraph 6, second paragraph -- on page 6, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: There was constant shooting at night from Serbian villages on Muslim villages. As a result of that constant intimidation and liquidations of certain Bosniaks - I mentioned some examples - and the awareness that Serbs were being armed by the SDS and the Yugoslav army, the people slowly started moving out -- or rather, some individuals who trusted those reports started moving out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not asking you about the fire coming from Serbian villages against Muslim villages, as you are claiming. I'm asking you about this when you personally opened fire. You weren't opening fire from a Serbian village, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: No. That happened in front of my father's house. I went out in the evening with another three friends of mine --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your brother-in-law Sabit Mujkic, the former commander of the TO, et cetera, you were all armed, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know about them. I really don't know. But there was a burst of fire from the darkness at a distance of 150 metres. I got very scared. I didn't know what to do. I fired a shot with my pistol. After that, the shooting stopped and we managed to escape into Mahala in the darkness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you say they were firing from a distance of 150 metres? Is that what you said? Or did they fire 150 bullets?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: From a distance of 100 to 150 metres. It was dark. I don't know the exact distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were they firing at?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: They were firing at us, who had just left my father's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But no one was hurt or hit.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Of course not. And it's a good thing that nobody was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that that was normal, that means that nobody wanted to target you.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that, in view of how it looked, and we heard the bullets whizzing by and hitting some buildings around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So they fired at you, a whole burst of fire from 100 to 150 metres, and no one was hurt? Very well. On page 5, sixth paragraph, you say it was surprising to what extent each Serb without any exception changed and started to hate Muslims. What do you think -- first of all, is what you're saying really true, or was that perhaps in reaction to what the SDA was doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: The SDA really didn't do anything so awful or bad, nor did it give any cause to provoke such a reaction on the part of the Serb people towards the Muslim people. This was simply the result of systematic preparations by the Serb people to separate from the Muslim people, to get armed, to prepare themselves, and finally to occupy Bratunac municipality and to expel the Muslims and to kill a large number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember that sometime in April 1992 units of the JNA started to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly when that happened, whether there was any withdrawal of JNA units from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I really don't remember that. But I do remember that there were some withdrawals of JNA units from Croatia and that they arrived with great frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You don't remember that. But do you remember that there was an order from the top echelons of the Muslim part of Bosnia and Herzegovina to block, prevent, and attack units of the JNA that were leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. I don't remember that there was any such order. If it had existed, I would probably know if any such thing had existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you would know.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, possibly. I assume I would have heard it from someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will quote now. "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Ministry of Defence, TO Headquarters Sarajevo, April 1992. Sarajevo. Order about the implementation of the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," number so and so, 0211327/92, which doesn't matter anyway, "the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," then the number I mentioned, "regarding the withdrawal of JNA units from the territory of BH, and because of violations of this Presidency decision and the beginning of plundering of the property of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the former JNA, I order to carry out complete and large-scale prevention and blocking of all roads in BH along which JNA units are withdrawing materiel in coordination with MUP. "Secondly, blockade the surroundings of military facilities from which technical materiel is being withdrawn." So this means that the JNA is withdrawing together with its equipment and materiel and it is -- the response is that it should leave that materiel behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you go on -- before you go on reading. Do you know what the accused is talking about at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Ray I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the order of Commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't ask this witness. If he doesn't know anything about it, it's a pointless activity. No doubt you can ask some other witness or get it in in some other way. But asking this witness about it, who knows nothing, is pointless.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, have you noticed that the witness said a moment ago - and I am paraphrasing his sentence - that if any such thing existed, he would have known? Which is quite logical in view of the function that he performed in the Party of Democratic Action. Therefore, as he says that he would have known if any such thing existed, I am now showing him that such a thing did exist, and he now says that he doesn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Look, you can produce it with some other witness, but it's pointless arguing about this witness -- about something he knows nothing about. We're just wasting time. Now, move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, do you know of the order of the Minister of Internal Affairs Alija Delimustafic, dated also April 1992, ordering complete and large-scale blocking of all roads in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina along which units of the former JNA are logging their withdrawal and pullout of equipment and materiel in collaboration with MUP?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I have to say again that I know nothing about that order. And let me remind you that on the 17th of April, 1992 I left Bratunac. You keep saying that this happened in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It could have been before the 17th of April and it could be after the April.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: That is quite true. That is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing from the moment you left Bratunac on the 17th of April. From the 17th of April, you know nothing about Bratunac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I do know some things, but I don't know about the things you've just asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Up until the 17th of April and inclusive, not a single bullet was fired over there. Bratunac was not captured by force on the 17th of April. There was no shooting. There was no fire. This is what you told Mr. Kwon in answer to a question of his. So you don't know anything about Bratunac when anyone was firing any shots, and you don't know anything about these orders either. Is that right, Mr. Gusic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Let us be specific: I said that on the 17th of April, while I was present in Bratunac - and this was up until 16 or 1700 hours, I don't know exactly - there was no shooting where I was, and that was in the urban part of Bratunac. As for before the 17th of April, I said several times that there was constant shooting at night from Serbian villages against Muslim villages and that there was even a calling that the Serbs from Kravica ambushed and killed two Muslims and wounded two others. I think I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that under those tense circumstances, on the 4th of April the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the complete name in those days was the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in incomplete composition, without Serb representatives, took a decision on the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence, the police, and the civil defence? This was on the 4th of April. Do you remember that decision?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I do remember that decision, a decision on mobilisation. Of course, I don't know whether the Presidency was complete or not. I don't know the details about the decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you don't know that that decision was arbitrarily adopted exclusively by Muslim and Croat members even though BH was still a part of SFRY in those days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No point wasting time on these things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that on the 6th of April, Germany and then the European Union recognised the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its separation from the Yugoslav state on the basis of a referendum held again without the participation of the Serbs? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does the rule still apply that the three nations over there are equal in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no. Not a question for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, do you remember, that on the 12th of April, that is, less than seven days after the recognition of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, Izetbegovic ordered an all-out and unprovoked attack on Yugoslav army facilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you about those details. Perhaps you should ask President Izetbegovic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you now explain to me, please, your statement on page 6, paragraph 6. You said that on the 17th of April, a Serbian military unit arrived in town, that soldiers in JNA uniforms told you that it was a Serb municipality, that they were armed and organised and supported by the army. Those are your words I'm quoting. So if this was the JNA, if they were members of the JNA, could they say that they were supported by the JNA? Could you explain that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. On the 17th of April, Miroslav Deronjic came to the police station and said that military units -- some military units, some formations had entered Bratunac and that the officers in charge of those units had said that we should go to the Fontana, that they were waiting for us, and if we didn't come, they would know what to do. When we got there, some of those officers were wearing uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army; others were wearing camouflage uniforms. I don't know exactly what kind of officers they were and what kind of units they headed, but I do know that they said, among other things, "Bratunac is a Serb municipality. Serb laws must apply here. We want to establish Serb authority." They said they were just the forerunners and that the rest of the unit was in Ljubovija. As I was in a corner, as we were leaving, I heard one of them, one of these officers, telling another, "The unit in Ljubovija should be told that they need not come to Bratunac today. There are about one and a half thousand of them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this sentence, you say - and I quote your sentence - "They told us that they were armed, well organised, and that they were supported by the army." This is what you say in your statement. So this was obviously some kind of local Territorial Defence claiming that they enjoyed the support of the army. They never -- you never mentioned the things you're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, in the addendum. We'll talk about those. I understand that we have to adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more time do I have for tomorrow? Would you be kind enough to tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only twenty minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Didn't you say that I would have the time I would normally have had the examination-in-chief not been shortened unexpectedly? And as you see for yourself, the plan was that it should take three hours. So I had reckoned with at least those three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, three hours was the total time which was estimated for the witness. What we have allowed you is one hour and three-quarters, which we think more than sufficient. Could you be back, please, Mr. Gusic, at 9.00 tomorrow morning. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.49 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday the 6th day of May, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
